habit_line: Focus habit: Check - Ask the child to test a second case before saying it works. Say: “Will it work with a different number? Test it.” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Today you are code-breakers. Spies, generals and computers all hide messages with codes. The oldest one we know is over 2000 years old, and it runs on the same maths as a clock.
Notice it. Test it. Explain why. Today “test it” means: crack it, then let the computer check.
do: Focus habit: Check - Ask the child to test a second case before saying it works. Say: “Will it work with a different number? Test it.” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Look at the clock. It is 9 o’clock. What time will it be 4 hours later? How did you work it out?
Now 11 o’clock and 13 hours later. Did you go past 12? What happened?
With a shift of 3, A becomes D and B becomes E. What do you think Z becomes? Write your guess before you make the strip.
stuck: Stuck making the strip: write A to Z on one line. Underneath, start at D under A, and keep going.
Stuck at the end of the alphabet: “After Z, where does the bottom row carry on?”
Finished early: invent a shift, code a short message for your partner, and give them only one clue.

say: “It is 9 o’clock. I count on 5 hours: 10, 11, 12, 1, 2. Adding gives 14, but a clock wraps round after 12, so 14 − 12 = 2. In maths we write 14 mod 12 = 2: the remainder when 14 is divided by 12.”
“To code Z with shift 5: Z is 25. 25 + 5 = 30. There is no letter 30, so I wrap round: 30 − 26 = 4, and 4 is E.”
“To decode A with shift 4: A is 0. 0 − 4 = −4. Below zero, so I add 26: −4 + 26 = 22, and 22 is W.”

do: Ask: “What number is that letter? Did you start at A = 0?”
Ask: “Your number went past 25. What do you do?”
Ask: “How can you check your code? Decode it again and see if you get back the message.”
stuck: Hint 1: “Change each letter to its number first. Use the strip.”
Hint 2: “Add the shift. If you go past 25, take away 26.”
Hint 3: “To decode, take away the shift. If you go below 0, add 26.”

say: “Why does a shift of 26 change nothing?”
“Ali says decoding shift 3 is the same as coding again with shift 23. Is he right? Why?”
ask: “Why does a shift of 26 change nothing?”

A shift of 26 moves every letter once round the whole 26-letter clock, so each letter lands back on itself (26 mod 26 = 0). Ali is right: shifting back 3 and shifting forward 23 land on the same letter, because 23 + 3 = 26 is a full turn. For example D (3): 3 − 3 = 0 = A, and 3 + 23 = 26, 26 mod 26 = 0 = A.

say: “Today you used clock arithmetic to make and break codes, and you made the computer do it for you. Mathematicians call this modular arithmetic, and it helps protect messages sent on the internet. Well done, code-breakers!”

p6l8-title.note: Objective: Do clock arithmetic (counting past the end wraps round to the start), use n mod m as the remainder when n is divided by m, solve clock and calendar puzzles with mod 12 and mod 7, code and decode Caesar ciphers with letter numbers (A = 0 … Z = 25, code = (letter + shift) mod 26), crack a code, and test it all with a Scratch program that uses a list of letters and mod. Materials: A laptop or desktop with Scratch 3 open (the tutor shares the starter file L8_Code_Machine.sb3, which has a list called alphabet holding A to Z and the loop already built), mini whiteboards, paper for code strips, scissors. Online: Children make their code strips on paper and use them in the lesson (nothing is held up to the camera). The tutor reads out the coded names (nothing is held up to the camera); partners decode on paper. Pairs use breakout rooms for the coding part; the driver shares the screen. Starter project: the tutor shares the file L8_Code_Machine.sb3 (not a link only; children use File, Load from your computer, no account needed) containing the list alphabet with A to Z already filled in, and the loop already built; children add the three cipher blocks. Block colours on our slides are simplified; in Scratch, list blocks are red-orange (Variables palette) and you find blocks by the category name on the left, not by colour. Scratch set-up: the starter project is the file L8_Code_Machine.sb3 (sent to families with the workbook; the tutor keeps a copy and the answer key L8_Code_Machine_ANSWER.sb3): a list called alphabet holding the letters A to Z, and everything in the machine except the 3 cipher blocks. Children load it with File, Load from your computer. If a child has no file, build it from the whole-machine slide (add each letter with the add to list block). Scratch lists count from item 1, so letter number n (A = 0) is item n + 1. The mod block is in the Operators menu. List blocks in Scratch are red-orange and live in the Variables palette; our slides draw them as simple coloured shapes, so find blocks by the category name on the left, not by colour. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson, with a standing flex buffer): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6, warm-up 6 to 11.5, explore 11.5 to 26, mini-lesson 26 to 37 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 37 to 42, worksheet 42 to 73 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it, flex 73 to 77 (unscripted: use it for Think harder or catch-up; it is lost first), talk time 77 to 83, exit slip 83 to 86, looking back 86 to 88, close and stamp 88 to 90. SPINE: Today's tool is Spot the pattern. Find the rule, test it on a new case, then use it to jump far. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook. HABIT: Focus habit: Check. Ask the child to test a second case before saying it works. Say: "Will it work with a different number? Test it." Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

p6l8-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6. These are ideas we have not learnt yet: say so, and say that guessing and "I do not know" are welcome and nobody is marked. Read the two puzzles aloud. Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone can get a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle on today's idea. ONE check moment only: after both puzzles, everyone says the answers together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Never private chat. Never compare answers across children, never read wrong answers aloud. Then click to reveal the answers one after the other and move on with no reaction round: say each answer in 15 words or fewer, then say: "Both of these are what we learn today." Answers: Puzzle 1: 1 o’clock (8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 1). Counting on round the clock face works. Puzzle 2: Friday. 100 ÷ 7 leaves remainder 2 (98 is 14 full weeks), so move 2 days on from Wednesday: Thursday, Friday. Guessing and “I do not know” are fine. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: say "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Nobody is singled out. Any child can choose it and any child can go back. Never announce who is on which page and never say advanced or top group. Do not record this as a mark. Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

p6l8-warm1.note: Minutes 6 to 9. Four calls only (the day-of-the-week jump was cut). Show each question, give thinking time, write it, say the answer together on three, then click. 1) 10 o’clock. 2) 10 + 4 = 14, past 12, so 2 o’clock. 3) 3 − 5 = −2: go back 3 to 12, then 2 more to 10. 4) 12 hours is a full turn: back to 8. Ask: "What do you do when you go past 12?" (start again at 1). This wrapping round is today's big idea.

p6l8-warm2.note: Minutes 9 to 11.5. Whiteboards, then click. Three questions only. 1) 17 = 3 × 5 + 2. 2) 26 ÷ 26 = 1 remainder 0. 3) 40 = 3 × 12 + 4. Today we call the remainder "mod": 17 mod 5 = 2. Ask: "What are the only possible remainders when you divide by 5?" (0, 1, 2, 3, 4).

p6l8-explore1.note: Minutes 11.5 to 26 (this slide 11.5 to 16.5). The shifted alphabet strip is SHOWN on the slide (A above D), so nobody copies it out (this saves about 1.5 minutes). Children code their first names, swap, decode, then decode PDWK LV IXQ (MATH IS FUN). The highlighted X, Y, Z show the key moment: the bottom row runs out, so it wraps round to A, B, C. Do not explain this yet: ask "What happened at the end?" Online: the tutor reads out the coded names and partners decode on paper. If a pair wants more: invent your own shift and send a coded word with one clue. Go further what-if (not a slide: paste it in the chat for any pair that finishes early, and take it up only if a pair wants to share): What if the shift is 13? Code the word HELLO with shift 13. Then code your answer with shift 13 again. What do you notice? Predict first. Answer: HELLO becomes URYYB, and coding URYYB with shift 13 gives HELLO again. Two shifts of 13 make 26, a full circle of the alphabet.

p6l8-explore2.note: Minutes 16.5 to 26. Two questions (the shift-of-26 question is cut). Gather the pairs. Answers: 1) A, B and C: after Z the alphabet wraps round to the start. 2) Shift each letter back 3 (or forward 23). PDWK LV IXQ is MATH IS FUN. Link back to the clock: letters are a 26-hour clock.

p6l8-teach1.note: Minutes 26 to 27.5. Teach. Use a real clock or the picture. Click 1: the hand sweeps from 9 to 2. Click 2: the addition and subtracting a full turn. Click 3: the word "mod". Think-aloud: "It is 9 o’clock. I count on 5 hours: 10, 11, 12, 1, 2. Adding gives 14, but a clock wraps round after 12, so 14 − 12 = 2. In maths we write 14 mod 12 = 2: the remainder when 14 is divided by 12." Say: mod is just the remainder: 14 ÷ 12 = 1 remainder 2. Note: on a real clock we write 12 where maths writes 0; both mean the top of the clock.

p6l8-we1.note: Minutes 27.5 to 29.5. Click through; ask the group to predict before each reveal. Think-aloud: "45 days is 6 whole weeks and 3 days. The whole weeks do nothing, because after 7 days it is the same day again. So only the remainder matters: 3 days after Thursday is Sunday." Watch for: counting today as day 1 (that gives Saturday). Ask: "What day was it 45 days ago?" (Thursday − 3 = Monday).

p6l8-we2.note:
Minutes 29.5 to 31.5. Click through. Think-aloud: "To code Z with shift 5: Z is 25. 25 + 5 = 30. There is no letter 30, so I wrap round: 30 − 26 = 4, and 4 is E." Point out the highlighted letters on the strip: Z is above E, O above T. Ask: "Which letters wrap round with shift 5?" (V, W, X, Y, Z become A to E). Say: this is called a Caesar cipher after Julius Caesar, who used a shift of 3 to send orders. Optional Python version (for children who already know Python):
alphabet = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
message = "MEET AT THE MRT"
shift = 3
code = ""
for letter in message:
 if letter in alphabet:
 n = alphabet.index(letter) # A is 0
 m = (n + shift) % 26 # % is mod
 code = code + alphabet[m]
 else:
 code = code + letter # keep spaces
print(code)
Run as it is, it prints PHHW DW WKH PUW (MEET AT THE MRT with shift 3). Set shift = -3 and message = "PHHW DW WKH PUW" to decode (Python % gives a answer between 0 and 25 even for negative numbers).

p6l8-try2.note: Minutes 31.5 to 33. Whiteboards, then click. a) C 2 + 3 = 5 = F, A 0 + 3 = 3 = D, T 19 + 3 = 22 = W: FDW. b) Y 24 + 4 = 28, 28 mod 26 = 2 = C; E 4 + 4 = 8 = I; S 18 + 4 = 22 = W: CIW (the wrap-round case). c) Decoding subtracts: F 5 − 3 = 2 = C, R 17 − 3 = 14 = O, G 6 − 3 = 3 = D, H 7 − 3 = 4 = E: CODE. Ask: Which letters go below 0 when decoding with shift 3? (A, B and C: add 26.)

p6l8-we3.note:
Minutes 33 to 36. Click through the decoding steps, then the Scratch blocks. Think-aloud: "To decode A with shift 4: A is 0. 0 − 4 = −4. Below zero, so I add 26: −4 + 26 = 22, and 22 is W." Decoding with shift 4 is the same as coding with shift 22, because 26 − 4 = 22. The blocks run once for each letter of the message: "for each letter" is a repeat loop. The whole machine (folded into this slide): the starter project already has the list alphabet and the loop (ask for the message; code starts empty; i counts the letters; repeat once for each letter of the answer; take letter i; if the letter is in the list code it, else copy it so spaces survive; add 1 to i; say the code), and children add only the 3 cipher blocks inside the if. Without the if a space gives item # of 0, n = -1 and a wrong letter. Type capitals. Open the starter and code HELLO live (about 2 minutes, because the list is already there). Optional Python version (for children who already know Python):
alphabet = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
message = "MEET AT THE MRT"
shift = 3
code = ""
for letter in message:
 if letter in alphabet:
 n = alphabet.index(letter) # A is 0
 m = (n + shift) % 26 # % is mod
 code = code + alphabet[m]
 else:
 code = code + letter # keep spaces
print(code)
Run as it is, it prints PHHW DW WKH PUW (MEET AT THE MRT with shift 3). Set shift = -3 and message = "PHHW DW WKH PUW" to decode (Python % gives a answer between 0 and 25 even for negative numbers).

p6l8-key.note: Minutes 36 to 37. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Off by one: counting A as 1 in the maths (we use A = 0, Z = 25), or forgetting that Scratch’s list starts at item 1. (2) Not wrapping round: writing a number bigger than 25 (or below 0 when decoding) instead of taking away or adding 26. (3) Calendars: counting today as day 1 (Saturday + 2 days is Monday, not Sunday), or giving the quotient instead of the remainder for mod.

p6l8-break.note: Minutes 37 to 42. 5 minutes. Online: children stay in view of the camera. The 12-hour sweep returns the arm to the same place: that is 12 mod 12 = 0.

p6l8-ws1.note: Minutes 42 to 53. In pairs. Show this preview, do not read it aloud. Walk around. Ask "How do you know?" before giving any help. For Q2 check pairs write the letter numbers first and wrap round with 26.

p6l8-ws1ans.note: Minutes 53 to 56. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q2 (code and decode with the shift), about 35 seconds a question. Q1: a) 8 + 7 = 15, 15 − 12 = 3. b) 30 mod 12 = 6, 11 + 6 = 17, 17 − 12 = 5. c) 4 − 9 = −5, + 12 = 7. d) 100 mod 7 = 2 (98 = 14 weeks), Saturday + 2 = Monday. e) 30 mod 7 = 2, Saturday back 2 = Thursday. f) 29 mod 12 = 5, 50 mod 7 = 1 (49 = 7 × 7), 100 mod 26 = 22 (78 = 3 × 26). Q2a: P 15 → 22 = W, I 8 → 15 = P, Z 25 → 32 mod 26 = 6 = G, A 0 → 7 = H. Q2b: M 12 − 10 = 2 = C, Y 24 − 10 = 14 = O, N 13 − 10 = 3 = D, O 14 − 10 = 4 = E.

p6l8-teachtrace.note: Minutes 56 to 58.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q3 traces WAY with shift 5; this is a different word). Click to add each row: S = 18 → 28 → 2 = C; K = 10 → 20 = U; Y = 24 → 34 → 8 = I. Ask: "Which letter needed the mod?" (S and Y, because the number went past 25). A trace table is how programmers check code by hand.

p6l8-teachcrack.note: Minutes 58.5 to 61. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 cracks a different message by finding a repeated 3-letter word). Think-aloud: "A short word is the best clue. A two-letter word that makes sense is IS, IT, IN, AT, OF. If NX is IS, N went to I, so the shift is 5 backwards. Then I test it on the other words." Show the crack program (Python): for shift in range(1, 26) prints every shift: the one that reads as English wins. In Scratch: repeat 25, change shift by 1, decode and say. This is called brute force.

p6l8-ws2.note: Minutes 61 to 70. Children work alone on Q3 and Q4 (they may test in Scratch); Q5 (two shifts in a row) is the take-home question, marked with a star in the workbook. Show this preview, do not read it aloud. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson.

p6l8-ws2ans.note: Minutes 70 to 73. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q4 (cracking the code). Q5 is the take-home question: its answer is here so children can mark it at home, and you take it up at the start of the next lesson (shifts add like jumps on a 26-hour clock: 15 then 15 is 4; the shift that undoes 15 is 11). Q4: the repeated word BPM; "the" is the most common 3-letter word; T = 19, B = 1: 19 + 8 = 27, 27 mod 26 = 1. Decode every letter by 8 back (or forward 18): BPM SMG QA CVLMZ BPM UIB is THE KEY IS UNDER THE MAT. Q5: a) 6 + 9 = 15. b) 19 + 12 = 31, 31 mod 26 = 5. c) 9 + 17 = 26, a full turn. d) Shift 13 used twice is 26: ROT13 is a real code, and coding twice decodes it.

p6l8-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. For children who finish early (not on the worksheet). Answers: 1) Tuesday and Wednesday (365 = 52 × 7 + 1, 366 = 52 × 7 + 2) 2) Yes: 29 mod 26 = 3, so a shift of 29 is a full turn (26) plus 3. 3) 11, 11 and 10. Adding the remainders and taking mod 12 again gives the same answer: (11 + 11) mod 12 = 22 mod 12 = 10.

p6l8-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) Two letters can give the same code letter: A (0) and N (13) both give 0 = A (13 × 2 = 26). So every code letter could stand for two different letters. 2) GAD (C = 2 gives 6 = G, A = 0 gives 0 = A, B = 1 gives 3 = D). No: all 26 letters get different code letters, because 3 and 26 have no common factor.

p6l8-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Q1: "What is 13 × 2? What letter is number 26 mod 26?" Q2: "Fill in the three code letters. Could two different letters ever give the same number?"

p6l8-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. Q1: doubling loses information: every code number is even, so only 13 different code letters can appear and each stands for two letters (n and n + 13). That is why a code must be able to be undone: the shift code always can. Q2: ×3 works because 3 and 26 share no common factor; ×13 or ×2 do not. Link: the clock with jumps of 5 (visits all 12 numbers) and jumps of 4 (does not) from the question bank.

p6l8-gap-cr1.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM cr1 (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "Letters stand for digits"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: Guess and check. SAY: A cipher replaces letters with other symbols, and so does this puzzle. Start with the column that cannot be wrong: the answer has 4 digits. ASK: What is the first letter of the answer? Which column do you do next, and what do you try? LISTEN FOR: A = 1. The ones and tens digits of the answer are the same letter, B, which gives two equations to test. Make a table of tries for C and E. This is Guess and check, not Spot the pattern, even though it sits in the Secret Codes lesson. Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: D = 5, E = 7, C = 3, A = 1, B = 4. Check: 573 + 771 = 1344. WHY: A = 1 (two 3-digit numbers add to less than 2 000). Ones: C + 1 = B, so there is no carry. Tens: E + E = 10 + B with a carry of 1. Hundreds: D + E + 1 = 10 + C. So B = C + 1 and 2E = 11 + C, which needs C odd. C = 1 is used by A; C = 3 gives E = 7, B = 4 and D = 5; C = 5 gives D = B = 6 and C = 7 gives D = C, which break the rule. Check: 573 + 771 = 1344.

p6l8-gap-cr2.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM cr2 (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "Letters stand for digits, a longer one"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: Guess and check. SAY: What is the first letter of the answer? Then look for a column where a letter added to itself or to a known digit has only a few possible answers. ASK: Which letter must be 0? Why? How do you check your answer against every column? LISTEN FOR: A = 1 from the size of the sum. Ones: E + D = 11. Tens: D + C + 1 = E. Combine them: 2 x D + C = 10. Children use a table of tries for C and D. Accept any organised method that checks all four columns. Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: B = 9, D = 5, E = 6, A = 1, C = 0. Check: 956 + 105 = 1061. WHY: A = 1. Ones: E + D = 10 + A = 11. Tens: D + C + 1 = E. So 2D + C = 10. Hundreds: B + A = 10 + C, so B = 9 + C and C = 0, D = 5, E = 6, B = 9. Check: 956 + 105 = 1061 and ACEA reads 1, 0, 6, 1. This is the only solution (checked by a script).

p6l8-gap-last.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM last (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "Last digit of a power"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: Spot the pattern. SAY: Only the last digit matters. Write the last digit of 2, 2 × 2, 2 × 2 × 2, ... and look for the repeat. Then use the clock arithmetic idea: what is 45 on a clock of the cycle length? ASK: How long is the cycle for 2? For 3 (the last digit of 13)? How does a remainder tell you where you land? LISTEN FOR: 2: 2, 4, 8, 6, cycle of 4. 45 = 11 × 4 + 1, so the 1st in the cycle: 2. 3: 3, 9, 7, 1, cycle of 4. 30 = 7 × 4 + 2, so 9. Listen for "remainder after dividing by the cycle length". Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) 2. (b) 9. WHY: Last digits of powers of 2 repeat 2, 4, 8, 6. 45 mod 4 = 1, so 2. Only the last digit of 13 matters, which is 3: 3, 9, 7, 1 repeat. 30 mod 4 = 2, so 9. SAME SKILL, NEW NUMBERS (tutor bank, say it aloud or write it on the board): Find the last digit of 7²⁰²⁶. Answer: 9 (the cycle is 7, 9, 3, 1 and 2 026 mod 4 = 2).

p6l8-talk.note: Minutes 77 to 83. Both questions are kept in this lesson (it has 4 minutes of flex). Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Second question: Ali says decoding shift 3 is the same as coding again with shift 23. Is he right? Why? Answer: A shift of 26 moves every letter once round the whole 26-letter clock, so each letter lands back on itself (26 mod 26 = 0). Ali is right: shifting back 3 and shifting forward 23 land on the same letter, because 23 + 3 = 26 is a full turn. For example D (3): 3 − 3 = 0 = A, and 3 + 23 = 26, 26 mod 26 = 0 = A. Praise the reasons, not only the answers.

p6l8-exit.note: Minutes 83 to 86. Answer: GH (H = 7, 7 + 25 = 32, 32 mod 26 = 6 = G; I = 8, 33 mod 26 = 7 = H). A shift of 25 is the same as shifting back 1, because 25 = 26 − 1. Extension: The starter already keeps spaces (if the letter is in the alphabet list, code it, else join the letter itself). Add a “crack” button that says the message decoded with every shift from 1 to 25.

p6l8-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 86 to 88. Start the timer (75 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new. HABIT: Focus habit: Check. Ask the child to test a second case before saying it works. Say: "Will it work with a different number? Test it." Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.
